report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported. For pregnant people with chronic HBV and high viraemia (typically HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) started at about 28–32 weeks’ gestation lowers the residual risk of mother-to-child transmission *when combined with standard infant prophylaxis* (timely hepatitis-B birth-dose vaccine, completion of the vaccine series, and—where indicated/available—HBIG).

A pivotal randomized trial in high-viral-load mothers found lower infant infection with maternal TDF begun at 30–32 weeks (4.7% vs 18.2% by intention-to-treat analysis); this underpins recommendations. WHO recommends TDF from week 28 until at least delivery at HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL. Evidence is not entirely uniform: a Thai placebo-controlled trial found very low transmission with excellent, immediate infant immunoprophylaxis even without TDF, so the absolute added benefit depends on baseline transmission risk and quality/timing of newborn prevention.

TDF is therefore an adjunct—not a replacement—for neonatal immunoprophylaxis. Management should include HBV DNA testing, obstetric/hepatology input, and monitoring after stopping therapy because postpartum hepatitis flares can occur.

Sources:  
- https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1508660  
- https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/978-92-4-000270-8  
- https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1708131
